docs.title: Logistics
docs.text: How the world's stuff actually moves — and how supply chains get inspected, evaded, and attacked.

docs.title: Case Study: The Al Habsi Network — Iranian Oil, Chinese Buyers, American Banks
docs.text:
In Logistics 101 I sketched the anatomy of a sanctions-evasion scheme in the abstract: dark AIS, ship-to-ship transfers, forged bills of lading, shell ownership. This post takes apart a real, indicted network that allegedly ran that entire playbook end to end — the case of Mahmood Rashid Amur Al Habsi, the Omani oil trader on the FBI's wanted list, and his partner Wang Shaoyun, wanted on the same warrant.

This is a deep dive built on primary sources: the 12-count federal indictment (United States v. Shaoyun Wang and Mahmood Rashid Amur Al Habsi, 1:24-cr-00049, D.D.C.), the DOJ press release, OFAC's 2021 designation of the network, the FBI wanted pages, and the Rewards for Justice listing offering up to $15 million. An indictment is an allegation — both defendants are fugitives, presumed innocent until proven guilty.

One note before the mechanics: every record in this case describes private individuals using private companies. Nothing in the public record implicates the Sultanate of Oman or its government in this scheme — the companies were simply registered there, the way shells are registered in Liberia, Gibraltar, and the Marshall Islands throughout this story.

docs.title: The principals
docs.text:
Role Who Supply side Mahmood Rashid Amur Al Habsi, Omani, b. 1984 — oil trader; ran acquisition, shipping, and document fraud through his own companies Demand side Wang Shaoyun, Chinese, b. 1969 — director of a Shandong refinery, chair of a Las Vegas company, general manager of its Hong Kong parent; negotiated with buyers and, allegedly, senior IRGC officials The client Rostam Ghasemi (a.k.a. Qasemi) — senior IRGC-Qods Force figure, previously Iran's oil minister, US-designated since 2019; per the indictment, the network operated for his benefit, on a 70/30 revenue split

The window ran December 2019 to July 2021. The scale the indictment pleads: an allocation letter authorizing up to 10 million barrels per month for five years.

docs.title: The corporate scaffolding
docs.text:
Before a single barrel moved, the network built its ownership maze — the "scrub the identity" layer from the 101 post, precisely mapped by OFAC's designation:

PERSON AL HABSI oil trader · Oman COMPANY Nimr International LLC Oman · Iraq · UAE COMPANY Nimr International SRL Romania COMPANY Bravery Maritime Corp Liberia · Dubai COMPANY Orbit Petrochemicals Oman · trading arm TANKER M/T Oman Pride IMO 9153525 · VLCC PERSON WANG SHAOYUN front companies · Las Vegas · HK ORGANIZATION IRGC-QODS FORCE · Ghasemi the client · 70% split rounded = person · square = company · dashed orange = sanctioned client

The graph, as the indictment and OFAC tell it:

  • Al Habsi → Nimr International L.L.C. (Muscat; active branches in Iraq and the UAE) → Orbit Petrochemicals Trading LLC (Oman) — the trading stack
  • Al Habsi → Bravery Maritime Corporation (Liberia, addressed in Dubai) — the shipping vehicle, registered owner of the tanker
  • Al Habsi → Nimr International S.R.L. (Romania) — a European arm
  • Wang's side: a US company in Las Vegas, its Hong Kong parent, and affiliates across China, Oman, and Turkey

Four jurisdictions to incorporate in, none of them the one where the cargo was born or sold.

docs.title: The fleet
docs.text:
Rewards for Justice lists the vessels below. The indictment shows how they were actually used — and the split is the interesting part:

Side Vessels Job Iranian-flagged (NITC-operated) Dino I, Dune Lift the crude from Iranian terminals Foreign-flagged commercial Oman Pride, Niovi, Carmen, Athina II, Escapade Buffer, receive at sea, or load direct and run dark to China

The buyer's ships never touch Iran. The buffer ship does — and the handoff happens at sea, engine to engine. Kharg and Sirri load the Oman Pride; somewhere around the Gulf of Oman the cargo crosses into the Niovi and the Carmen, which carry it on to China as 'Omani' crude. The Escapade skipped the handoff — it loaded directly and sailed dark:

ARABIAN SEA BAY OF BENGAL SOUTHCHINA SEA Kharg Sirri STS HANDOFF Jul & Sep 2020 Yantai Qingdao Lanshan Oman Pride · buffer tanker, loads at Sirri & Kharg Niovi → Yantai · ~1.8M bbl · ~$73M · Jul 2020 Carmen → Lanshan · ~1.8M bbl · ~$66M · Sep 2020 Escapade → Qingdao · AIS off · ~$37M · Feb 2020 map: coastlines Natural Earth · routes schematic · STS position approx. CHINESE BUYERS Chinese refineries US BANKS $8.5M BLOCKED Jul 1, 2021 $10M SHELLS Marshall Is · UK 70 / 30 Iranian parent Chinese partner $10M got through in June 2021 — the $8.5M wire on Jul 1 didn't

docs.title: The operations, voyage by voyage
docs.text:
The indictment pleads specific cargoes. Read as a logistics log:

Date Event Feb 7–12, 2020 Escapade loads ~733,616 barrels near Kharg Island (~$37M), bound for Qingdao Feb 6, 2020 — the day before An Al Habsi company emails the Escapade's captain "important instructions": switch off AIS and LRIT after exiting the Strait of Hormuz, for the entire voyage Jun 16, 2020 Al Habsi's Liberian company takes a $16.5M loan from US financial companies to buy a tanker — the future Oman Pride Jul 18–19, 2020 Oman Pride loads Iranian oil at Sirri Island Jul 23–24, 2020 STS: Oman Pride transfers ~1.8M barrels (~$73M) to the Niovi Aug 18–20, 2020 Oman Pride loads at Kharg; STS with NITC's Dune Sep 8–11, 2020 STS: ~1.8M barrels (~$66M) to the Carmen Oct 20, 2020 STS with NITC's Dino I; cargoes comingled with same-day Kharg oil Nov 8–29, 2020 Athina II transfers; backload to Oman Pride of 190,000 tons of "crude blend" — demanded directly by Ghasemi Nov 7, 2020 – Jan 2021 Deliveries: Niovi discharges at Yantai; Carmen at Lanshan — both Chinese ports

The concealment stack, exactly as the 101 post ordered it: AIS dark (the captain's orders in writing), STS laundering (breaking the port-to-port chain), comingling (deniable fractions), bribes (per Treasury's designation).

docs.title: The paper
docs.text:
The forgery layer is where the case gets almost funny. To sell Iranian Light as Omani crude:

  • Bills of lading for the Carmen and Niovi falsely stated Oman as origin, with Al Habsi's company as shipper.
  • The product was marketed as "Oman Crude Blend."
  • Buyers received spec sheets for "Omani Light Crude Oil" that were, in the indictment's words, "identical in all respects" to a 2017 NIOC spec sheet for Iranian Light — the forgery was a copy-paste of the real document.
  • A Certificate of Quality came from Geochem Middle East, a legitimate inspection firm — the network simply inserted itself as the client, laundering credibility along with cargo.

And the client relationship was barely hidden. In November 2020, per the indictment, Ghasemi emailed Al Habsi's company identifying himself as "IRGC Qods Force Deputy," called the Oman Pride cargo "our cargo," and demanded a backload. The beneficiaries were directing operations by email.

docs.title: The money
docs.text:
Dollars, through American banks — the stage that killed everything:

  • Laundering counts span wires of $2.2M, $1.0M, $1.8M, $3.3M (2020) and $7.4M, $6.7M, $14.0M, $2.2M, $4.6M, $8.5M (2021), routed through shell companies in the Marshall Islands, the UK, and elsewhere, with US banks misled about the source.
  • Revenue split: 70% to the Iranian side, 30% to Wang's company.
  • July 1, 2021: a US bank blocked the refinery's $8,512,218.90 wire under E.O. 13224. Within weeks, by Treasury's account, the Oman Pride sat idle at anchorage. The scheme was over.

docs.title: How it unraveled
docs.text:
The referee playbook, executed
  • Corporate graph traversal (Aug 13, 2021): OFAC designated Al Habsi and all four companies in one action — Nimr, Orbit, Bravery Maritime, Nimr SRL — plus the Oman Pride itself, under E.O. 13224.
  • Financial forensics: the US-bank paper trail, including the $16.5M tanker loan, gave HSI Washington and FBI Minneapolis documents, witnesses, and jurisdiction.
  • The indictment (Jan 25, 2024; unsealed Feb 2): 12 counts — IEEPA and sanctions violations, money-laundering conspiracy — and a seizure warrant for ~$8.5M.
  • The manhunt (Jun 12, 2025): FBI wanted pages for both; State Department RFJ offer up to $15 million. Both remain fugitives.

docs.title: The afterlife of a sanctions vessel
docs.text:
Here is the part that makes the case a classic. The star tanker — IMO 9153525 — did not die with the scheme. Public vessel databases (VesselFinder, UANI's tracker, OFAC's own records) let you watch its identity cycle:

Oman Pride (2020, Liberia) → Pride (2022, St Kitts) → Rider 1 (2022, Palau) → Lemur (2023, Cameroon) → Lydya N (2023, Palau) → Lillian (2025) → Sokolo (2026)

Nine names, six flags, one IMO number — which never changes, and which is how anyone paying attention keeps finding it:

FRONT VISTA 2004 · Marshall Is DEWI MAESWARA 2010 · Indonesia OMAN PRIDE 2020 · Liberia · OFAC designates 2021 PRIDE 2022 · St Kitts RIDER 1 2022 · Palau LEMUR 2023 · Cameroon LYDYA N 2023 · Palau · OFAC designates again 2025 LILLIAN 2025 SOKOLO 2026 IMO 9153525 one hull · one number · nine names

In March 2025, OFAC designated the same hull again — now called Lydya N, now property of a Seychelles shell, in the same action that hit Iran's oil minister and the Russia-linked shadow fleet. Per Ukraine's sanctions registry, it was later sold to a Crimea-linked owner. A tanker built for one evasion economy graduated into another. One hull, two wars.

The other vessels scattered similarly: NITC's Dino I and Dune were separately designated (2024, 2025) for Iran-related transfers; the Carmen sails today under yet another name; the Niovi — Greek-owned, Panama-flagged — was seized by Iran's own IRGC Navy in the Strait of Hormuz in May 2023, while reportedly entangled in a legal dispute with Al Habsi's Nimr International over a suspect cargo. In this world, even the subcontractors get hijacked.

docs.title: The logistics read
docs.text:
1. The scheme was logistics-complete. Owned tonnage, a two-tier fleet, a four-jurisdiction corporate stack, document fraud, and payment routing — every layer from the 101 post, purpose-built. This is what "heavy logistics skills" means in practice: not genius, but competent systems engineering pointed at an illegal supply chain.
  2. The IMO number is the tell. Names, flags, owners, and registries all rotate — the immutable identifier is the one the network can't change. Every serious investigator pivots on it; so does every serious registry-hopper failure.
  3. The weak link was money, not ships. AIS tampering and STS worked as designed. The dollar clearing system was the node the network couldn't route around — and the $8.5M blocked wire is where the story ends.
  4. Sanctions evasion is a renewable industry. The same hull served Iran's evasion economy and then Russia's. The skills, the shells, and even the steel are transferable — which is why vessel-tracking OSINT tracks hulls, not headlines.

docs.title: Logistics 101: The Field That Runs the World
docs.text:
Every field of security research eventually bends toward the same question: how does the thing actually get from A to B? Malware analysts trace supply chains of software. Intelligence analysts trace supply chains of weapons and oil. Sanctions enforcers trace supply chains of money — which is just cargo that moves faster.

Logistics is the discipline that answers that question. This post is a field guide: what logistics actually is, its major branches, and — because this is a security blog — how each branch gets inspected, gamed, and attacked. Think of it as recon on an entire industry.

docs.title: What logistics actually is
docs.text:
The classical definition is the seven Rs: getting the right product, in the right quantity, in the right condition, to the right place, at the right time, to the right customer, at the right cost. Miss any one of the seven and the operation failed, even if the cargo arrived.

Every logistics system, from Amazon to a sanctions-evasion network, decomposes into three primitives:

  • Nodes — fixed points where cargo rests or changes hands: ports, warehouses, airports, factories, transshipment hubs.
  • Links — the routes between them: sea lanes, air corridors, rail lines, roads, pipelines.
  • Modes — how cargo physically moves: container ship, bulk carrier, air freight, truck, rail, mule, dhow.

NODE port · warehouse LINK — the route MODE — ship · rail · truck · air NODE hub · buyer · port every logistics system — legal or not — is these three primitives, repeated

That's it. Everything else — customs brokers, bills of lading, freight forwarders, letters of credit, AIS transponders — is coordination overhead layered on top of nodes, links, and modes to make the seven Rs verifiable between parties who don't trust each other.

That last sentence is the whole reason this field matters to security people. Logistics is trust made mechanical. And anywhere trust is mechanical, it can be spoofed, forged, or bought.

docs.title: The cast — and how each one gets gamed
Commercial / supply chain logistics
docs.text:
The big one: more than 80% of world trade by volume moves by sea. Container shipping, bulk commodities, tankers, air cargo, and the warehouse-and-truck "last mile" that puts it in your hands.

Commercial logistics runs on documents as much as ships. The bill of lading (B/L) is the key one: it's simultaneously a cargo receipt, a contract of carriage, and proof of ownership. Present the original B/L at destination, collect the goods. Banks finance shipments against these papers through letters of credit. In a very real sense, world trade is a document-processing system with ships attached.

How it gets gamed: the gray fleet playbook

The techniques below are all documented in US Treasury/OFAC designations, DOJ indictments, and UN Panel of Experts reporting. The anatomy of an evasion scheme:

  • Go dark. Ships carry an AIS transponder that broadcasts identity and GPS-derived position. The UN Panel of Experts on North Korea documented vessels switching AIS off before illicit ship-to-ship (STS) transfers of coal and fuel — the "dark period" is itself a detection signal.
  • Spoof the position. AIS is unauthenticated and trivially forged. Analysts (notably C4ADS in its work on North Korea's fleet) have caught vessels broadcasting fake AIS positions — appearing to sit in one port while physically transferring cargo elsewhere. Maritime-intelligence firms (e.g. Windward's published analyses) describe a commercial market in AIS manipulation — spoofing as a service.
  • Scrub the identity. "Flag-hopping" — repeatedly re-registering the ship under new flag states — plus layered shell ownership and repeated renames make beneficial ownership a maze. This is the modern "gray fleet": aging tankers with opaque owners, first observed at scale moving sanctioned Russian and Iranian crude.
  • Forge the paper. Falsified or forged bills of lading misdeclare origin ("this isn't Iranian crude, it's Omani blend"), enabling the cargo to enter legitimate finance. The DOJ's case against Omani broker Mahmood Al Habsi and Chinese national Wang Shaoyun alleges exactly this: Iranian oil relabeled and sold into the legal market, payments laundered through US banks.
  • Blend it. Mixing sanctioned cargo with clean product at a compliant port makes the tainted fraction statistically deniable — documented in Reuters reporting on Iranian crude blended in Malaysian waters before delivery to China, and in UN Panel of Experts reporting on blended petroleum exports.

The inspection side — how analysts catch this — is beautiful OSINT: AIS gap analysis, satellite imagery of STS transfers at known anchorage hotspots, hull-number mismatch (transponder says one ship, imagery shows another), and corporate-registry pivoting on shell owners. U.S. government sources on the Al Habsi case: FBI wanted page, DOJ press release, Rewards for Justice.

docs.title: Military logistics
docs.text:
The branch with the oldest pedigree — the word itself comes from war. Amateurs talk tactics; professionals talk logistics, because an army that can't be fed, fueled, and resupplied stops being an army. Military logistics is the same nodes/links/modes triad under an adversary trying to destroy your links.

How it gets gamed: proxy resupply

States under sanctions don't move cargo with flagged military transports — they outsource to deniable civilian logistics. UN Panel of Experts reporting on Iran has documented small arms and components moving to proxy forces via unremarkable civilian dhows and trucks across the Gulf and land corridors: no flags, no manifests, mixed in with legitimate fishing and trade traffic. The evasion principle is camouflage by context — make your link indistinguishable from the environment's normal traffic. It's the physical version of hiding a C2 channel in ordinary HTTPS.

docs.title: Humanitarian logistics
docs.text:
Moving food, medicine, and shelter into crisis zones — often the hardest logistics on Earth: destroyed infrastructure, no functioning customs authority, and armed actors at every node. Organizations like the WFP's logistics arm run entire shipping lines and airlifts.

How it gets gamed: aid diversion

The UN's own reporting (including UN Panel of Experts findings on Somalia and the WFP's 2019 partial suspension of food aid distributions in Yemen over diversion) documents aid diverted by armed groups and coordinated networks: siphoning from convoys, falsifying beneficiary lists, and taxing access to routes. The security lesson: in any low-trust environment, the distribution layer is the softest target — the last mile is where verification is weakest and local power structures interpose themselves.

docs.title: Event & reverse logistics
docs.text:
Two smaller but instructive branches. Event logistics moves enormous volumes on brutal one-shot deadlines (think Olympics or a military deployment). Reverse logistics is everything flowing backwards: returns, repairs, recycling, end-of-life.

How it gets gamed: returns fraud

Reverse flows are fraud magnets because legitimate reverse traffic is anomalous by nature — irregular, poorly documented, priced by disposal logic rather than market logic. Documented patterns include returns of stolen goods for cash, counterfeit-for-genuine swaps (buy real, return fake), and brute-force refund fraud — tracked annually in the NRF's National Retail Security Survey and prosecuted in organized retail-crime cases. It's the same principle as cargo blending: a channel with intentionally noisy baselines is where anomalies hide best.

docs.title: The referees: sanctions & export controls
docs.text:
Every red team needs a blue team. In logistics, that's the sanctions and export-control apparatus: OFAC in the US Treasury (which maintains the SDN list and designates evasion networks), the UN Security Council and its Panels of Experts (which investigate and publish), national customs authorities, and an ecosystem of open-source investigators — journalists, NGOs like C4ADS, and hobbyist vessel trackers — who do for shipping what bug bounty hunters do for software.

Their detection toolbox, from the public case literature:

  • AIS gap analysis — where did the transponder go quiet, and does the gap overlap a known STS hotspot?
  • Identity forensics — hull number, paint, and superstructure matching against the claimed identity (vessels get "plastic surgery" too).
  • Corporate graph traversal — shell-company chains across registries until a beneficial owner falls out.
  • Financial forensics — payment flows through correspondent banks that reveal the forged-paper trail.
  • Satellite tasking — revisit a suspicious anchorage and photograph the transfer.

It's a cat-and-mouse with real stakes: the mouse gets indicted, the cat gets a $15 million reward program.

docs.title: Where this is going
docs.text:
Everything above — dark AIS, STS transfers, forged bills of lading, shell ownership — isn't hypothetical. It's the alleged operating model of a real, indicted network.

In the next post I'll take apart the case of Mahmood Rashid Amur Al Habsi, the Omani oil broker on the FBI's wanted list: how a few hundred million dollars of Iranian crude allegedly moved from sanctioned wells to willing buyers, which of the tricks from this post the network used at each stage, and how investigators unpicked it. Logistics 101, graded on a real exam.
